extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, literary practitioners, and readers interested in essays and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative remarks (embedded in 18th-century essays) about producing natural-history writing, general authorship, and the practice of literary criticism; includes observations on what makes writing durable or ephemeral. Useful for writers thinking about craft, revision, and how critics judge work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firsthand field observation for natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: “Natural history is no work for one that loves his chair or his bed. Speculation may be pursued on a soft couch, but nature must be observed in the open air.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural-history writing requires direct, on-site observation and gathering of specimens (examples given: collecting glow-worms, snails, observing daisies, hearing owls, hunting insects, exploring mines and coal-pits). The author stresses active fieldwork rather than armchair speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefatigable pertinacity in collecting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The author reports having “collected materials with indefatigable pertinacity,” spending many years assembling observations and specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing rigorous natural-history work (and analogous research-based writing) requires long-term commitment and persistence — years of gathering, revisiting, and expanding the inquiry (seven years, then another year in mines, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer feedback but avoid paralysis by consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading sections to friends, the author found contradictory advice (one disliked disposition of parts, another the colours of the style) and resolved “to read no more, but to take my own way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit knowledgeable critique, but beware that excessive or conflicting advice can paralyze the work. Balance external suggestions with authorial judgement to avoid endless revision or loss of voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to marketability and practical publishing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Booksellers and patrons judge works by practical metrics: size, subscription potential, patronage, and current market conditions (examples: a bookseller saying 'a book of that size would never do', requests for subscriptions, offers conditional on procuring subscribers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider format, length, subscription/patronage strategies, and publishers' economic concerns when planning and submitting work — practical realities affect whether a completed work reaches readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer general principles for longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that writes upon general principles, or delivers universal truths, may hope to be often read, because his work will be equally useful at all times and in every country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce writing that endures, emphasize universal themes and general principles rather than narrowly topical matters. Universality sacrifices immediate sensational appeal for lasting usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical subjects gain quick readers but are ephemeral
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that writes upon temporary subjects, easily finds readers, and quickly loses them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing tied to contemporary events or narrow controversies can generate rapid interest and fame but typically declines as circumstances change; be mindful of the trade-off between immediacy and permanence (example: Hudibras’s topical satire becoming largely forgotten).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision is essential — 'the art of blotting'
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the maxims repeated by critics: “the great art is the art of blotting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective writing depends on rigorous editing and cutting; pruning and revising (blotting) are core artistic practices rather than mere afterthoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy nature — favour naturalness over rigid rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: A frequently stated critical position: “the chief business of art is to copy nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity and fidelity to observed human nature should guide composition. Overly pedantic adherence to abstract rules is criticized; natural representation of character and circumstance is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of critics' pedantry and received maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is described as easily accessible and prone to repetition of received opinions: critics repeat maxims (e.g., 'copy nature', 'art of blotting', 'keep nine years') and often form judgements from books and coffee-house talk rather than original insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should treat critics' pronouncements with caution — critics can be inconsistent, enamoured of rules, and influenced by fashion. Evaluate criticism for substance rather than authority or jargon (illustrated by the satirical figure Dick Minim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that criticism vents malignity with limited damage
rubrics_metrics.description: “This profession has one recommendation peculiar to itself, that it gives vent to malignity without real mischief. ... The poison ... fumes away in empty hisses, and malice is set at ease with very little danger to merit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that critical hostility often harms less than authors fear; criticism can be malicious but may not destroy true merit. This is both a caution to writers not to overvalue petty attacks and an observation about the social function of criticism.
